extracted.intended_audience: Users/authors of Isabelle/Isar theories and proofs (Isabelle/HOL users, theorem-prover practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and syntactic/structural rules for writing Isabelle/Isar theory sources and Isar proof texts, including canonical proof patterns, lexical and outer/inner syntax conventions, document preparation, and diagnostic commands. Targets authors producing human-readable formal proofs and theory documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculational reasoning style (have/also/finally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the pattern “have eq by (rule r)” and compose the chain of results via also/finally to build calculational proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning from basic axioms is often tedious. Produce instances of given rules (potentially symmetric) using have ... by (rule r) and compose a chain of results via also/ﬁnally. These steps may involve any of the transitivity rules declared (trans, forw_subst, back_subst). Occasional substitutions in calculations are adequate, but should not be over-emphasized. Avoid composing a chain solely by plain transitivity with replacements always in topmost position (example given showing unfolding vs explicit substitutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of transitivity/substitution rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When composing equalities use the declared transitivity and substitution rules (trans, forw_subst, back_subst) appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The calculational chains in examples use trans to combine results, forw_subst in some right_unit combinations, and back_subst in other calculational steps. Choose the appropriate trans/subst rule for the intended replacement direction rather than forcing all steps into a single transitivity application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer automated simplifier for equational reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: For realistic object-logics rely on the Simplifier rather than manual unfolding and substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than writing sequences like 'unfolding left_inv ..' repeatedly, set up the Simplifier and write 'by (simp only: left_inv)' etc. The Simplifier is the main automated tool for equational reasoning in Isabelle; use it to normalize equational problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare introduction/elimination attributes for rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotate rules with attributes like [intro], [elim], [dest] to reflect their canonical role and enable Isar proof structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules such as impI [intro], impD [dest], disjI1 [intro], disjE [elim], conjI [intro] are declared with attributes so Isar can present canonical proof outlines. Declaring rules according to their shape makes Isar proof texts straightforward to write and read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use canonical Isar reasoning patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the canonical Isar proof outlines that correspond to intro/elim/dest rules (e.g., impI: assumes A => B shows A -> B; disjE: assumes A ∨ B obtains A B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The documentation summarizes core first-order rules and shows how each rule maps to an Isar proof skeleton. Use these canonical patterns (assume/show, obtain/fix/then/show, proof ... next ... qed) so proofs follow standard readable outlines and tactic-less structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive convenient elimination rules (avoid eager projection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When basic destructors force early projection choices (e.g., conjD1/conjD2), derive a simultaneous elimination (conjE) to obtain both components at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conjunctive destructions have the disadvantage that decomposing A ∧ B involves an immediate decision which component should be projected. Derive and use A ∧ B ==> (A ==> B ==> C) ==> C (conjE) so you can obtain both A and B together and avoid awkward proof structure. Similar considerations apply to disjunction eliminations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical reasoning via locales
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce classical principles locally (via locale/classical assumption) instead of making the object-logic globally classical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the principle of classical contradiction as a local assumption (locale classical = assumes classical: (¬ C =⇒ C) =⇒ C). This allows deriving classical consequences (double negation, tertium non datur) without forcing the entire object-logic into classical perspective. Use 'obtains ¬ thesis' style to express the classical rule in Isar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier proof patterns (∀ and ∃)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat quantifiers as operators on predicates and follow standard Isar patterns: use obtain for ∃-elimination, fix for ∀-introduction, and show/have for conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declare All/Ex with [intro]/[dest]/[elim] rules (allI, allD, exI, exE). In proofs: use 'obtain x where ... using ‹∃ x. ...›' for ∃-elimination, 'fix y' and 'show B y' for ∀-introduction, etc. The documentation provides a step-by-step example mixing ∃-elimination and ∀-introduction with annotate comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for literate, human-readable Isar proof texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Express proofs declaratively and clearly; Isar asks the user to 'express himself adequately, aiming at proof texts of literary quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit Isar's structured proof language (assume/then/show/next/qed) rather than low-level tactic scripts. Avoid overemphasis on mechanical substitutions and chains and instead present reasoning in readable blocks; use canonical shapes to communicate intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the Isar outer/inner syntax distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Outer syntax is Isabelle/Isar theory source syntax; inner syntax is the logic's types and terms. Inner syntax entities must generally be quoted when used as atomic tokens in outer syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general rule, inner syntax entities may occur only as atomic entities within outer syntax; e.g., the string "x + y" and identifier z are legal term specifications in a theory, while unquoted x + y is not. Printed documents often omit quotes for readability via LaTeX macros, but authors should be aware of the inner/outer distinction and quote complex inner entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical rules and tokenization
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the three outer lexical token categories (major keywords, minor keywords, named tokens) and the longest-prefix tokenization rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major and minor keywords are disjoint; keywords override named tokens. When tokenizing, the lexer takes the longest prefix forming a valid token. Use quoted strings to escape identifiers that clash with keywords. Knowing these rules helps front-ends determine document structure without full parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier and unknown naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the prescribed forms for short_ident, long_ident, sym_ident and for unknowns (term_var/type_var) with dot/index notation (e.g., ?x.1 or ?x1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: term_var = ?short_ident, type_var = ?type_ident. If an unknown's index is 0 it may be omitted (e.g., ?x, ?x0, ?x.0 all refer to same unknown). Be mindful of allowed characters (letters, greek names as \<alpha>, subscripts, digits) and sym_ident alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strings, cartouches, verbatim and comments usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the correct constructs for text embedding: strings with escapes, altstring/backquotes, cartouches for arbitrary nested text, verbatim for raw text (cannot contain '*}'), and formal/document comments for documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartouches permit arbitrary nested blocks and are handy for document text (‹. . . ›). Source comments (* ... *) are removed after lexical analysis (not for documentation). Use formal comments (comment‹text›, ^cancel, ^latex) for typeset documentation; they are part of the document output and support antiquotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document antiquotations to include formal entities
rubrics_metrics.description: In document text, refer to formal entities via antiquotations like theory, thm, lemma, term, term_type, const, locale, ML, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiquotations are interpreted in the current theory/proof context and are the standard way to include and pretty-print formal objects within generated LaTeX document text (see section listing many antiquotations). Use print_antiquotations to inspect them in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use markup commands for document structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use chapter, section, subsection, text, txt, and text_raw to structure generated documents and map to corresponding LaTeX macros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: chapter/section/etc. mark headings and may be used anywhere. text/txt specify paragraphs typeset via isamarkuptext; text_raw injects raw LaTeX without surrounding markup. All markup text may include antiquotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagnostic commands to inspect context
rubrics_metrics.description: Use print_theory, print_definitions, print_methods, print_attributes, print_theorems, print_facts, find_theorems, find_consts, thm_deps, unused_thms, etc., to query and debug the theory/proof context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: print_theory prints main logical content (option ! for verbosity). find_theorems accepts criteria name:, intro, elim, dest, solves, simp:term, term:pattern and can negate criteria with '-' and limit results; duplicates removed by default (use with_dups). find_consts has type/name criteria. thm_deps prints immediate dependencies; unused_thms lists never-used theorems. Use these commands to discover and manage available facts and rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search criteria for find_theorems and find_consts
rubrics_metrics.description: When searching for theorems or constants, supply criteria like name:, intro, elim, dest, solves, simp:t, term:t or strict:ty/ty and use '-' to negate criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns may contain '*' wildcards; simp: selects rewrite rules whose left-hand side matches given term; term: matches theorems containing a pattern (with '_' and schematic variables). For find_consts, strict:ty matches types strictly, ty matches subtypes as well. Use these criteria to precisely filter search results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem specification forms and attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use axmdecl, thmdecl, thmdef, thm/thms with optional attributes and selections (a(i) or a(j-k)) or literal fact propositions (altstring/cartouche).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes may appear on left/right of theorem references and are applied to the immediately preceding fact. Omitting names means theorems are not stored but attributes still apply. Extra brackets around attributes (e.g., [[simproc a]]) abbreviate an in-place declaration with an internal dummy fact ignored later—useful with declare/using.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes argument syntax (semi-inner parsing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute arguments are parsed a second time; arguments may be atoms or bracketed lists, and attributes appear as [name args , ...].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atom categories include identifiers, type/id/var tokens, numbers, keywords, cartouches. Because attributes are semi-inner, ensure their arguments conform to the expected inner-language atom categories; nested bracketed args are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured specification syntax for eigen-contexts and multiple cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Express rules with explicit eigenscopes using 'B x if A x and ... for x', and separate multiple specifications by '|' to indicate distinct cases with their own inferred types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'for' to fix variables and '_' as anonymous locally-fixed variables. Multi-case specifications make per-case typing clear. Structured_spec elements let you express rule structure compactly in Isar grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positional and named instantiations; placeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify theorem instantiations positionally as sequence of terms or '_' placeholders, or named as v = t assignments for schematic variables; both term and type instantiations are admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '_' to skip positions in positional instantiations. Named instantiations distinguish type vs term by variable naming syntax. Remember to quote complex inner syntax when used as instantiation arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use term and prop patterns for schematics and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where propositions or term fragments occur, bind schematic variables via patterns '(is p1 ... pn)'; declare local variables x::τ and propositions a:ϕ via vars and props constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern binding works for both term and prop. Declarations can introduce multiple vars or props simultaneously; typing may be omitted due to type inference and naming omitted due to implicit references. Use fix/assume/obtains constructs to create local scopes consistent with these patterns.
